scenes.narration: The reputation of Thomas Jefferson was built in the middle, not at the edges. A prolific writer and philosopher, Jefferson was the primary author of the Declaration of Independence. His political philosophy formed the basis for Jeffersonian democracy, which dominated early American politics alongside federalism.

Somebody like Thomas Jefferson should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Jefferson remains celebrated as an icon of American political values, but is also controversial for being a lifelong slave owner. Born into a slave owning family in Shadwell, Virginia, Jefferson emerged as an ideological leader of the American Revolution through his fierce advocacy for civil liberties, including the freedoms of speech, religion, and thought.

The life of Thomas Jefferson begins far from where the story usually starts. He was elected to represent Virginia in the Second Continental Congress in 1775 and selected a member of the Committee of Five. Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence largely alone, and the document was unanimously passed by the Congress in 1776.

Thomas Jefferson was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Minister to France in 1785 by the Confederation Congress, maintaining the American–French alliance against the British. Secretary of State by President George Washington in 1790, helping administer Washington's policy of neutrality in European conflicts.

To understand where Thomas Jefferson ended up, start with where Thomas Jefferson began. Jefferson and his political ally James Madison founded the Democratic-Republican Party in 1792, centered on republicanism, individual rights, agrarianism, and limited government. Running against Federalist Party candidate John Adams in 1796, Jefferson finished with the second-highest number of votes and became Adams's vice president.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Thomas Jefferson ran through years nobody filmed. He ran again in 1800, winning against Adams, and in 1804 overwhelmingly defeating the Federalists' Charles Cotesworth Pinckney of South Carolina. Jefferson's presidency assertively defended the nation's shipping and trade interests against Barbary pirates and aggressive British trade policies, promoted a western expansionist policy with the Louisiana Purchase, which doubled the nation's geographic size, and reduced military forces and expenditures following successful negotiations with France.

Each stage of the life of Thomas Jefferson made the next stage possible. In his second presidential term, he was beset by difficulties at home, including the trial of his former vice president Aaron Burr. In 1807, Jefferson implemented the Embargo Act to defend the nation's industries from British threats to U.S. shipping, limit foreign trade, and stimulate the birth of American manufacturing.

The people who knew Thomas Jefferson young describe someone already restless. Jefferson is ranked among the upper tier of U.S. presidents both by scholars and in public opinion. Presidential scholars and historians have praised Jefferson's advocacy of religious freedom and tolerance, his peaceful acquisition of the Louisiana Territory from France, and his leadership in supporting the Lewis and Clark Expedition.

What Thomas Jefferson built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. They acknowledge his lifelong ownership of large numbers of slaves, but offer varying interpretations of his views on and relationship with slavery. Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743 (April 2, 1743, Old Style, Julian calendar), at the family's Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia.

By the time Thomas Jefferson reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Peter Jefferson moved his family to Tuckahoe Plantation in 1745 following the death of William Randolph III, the plantation's owner and Jefferson's friend, who in his will had named Peter guardian of Randolph's children. Jefferson began his education together with the Randolph children at Tuckahoe under tutors.

The rise of Thomas Jefferson was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Thomas' father Peter, who was self-taught and regretted not having a formal education, entered Thomas into an English school at age five. In 1752, at age nine, he attended a local school run by a Presbyterian minister and also began studying the natural world, which he grew to love.

Setbacks came early for Thomas Jefferson, and the response to them is the real story. He was taught from 1758 to 1760 by the Reverend James Maury near Gordonsville, Virginia, where he studied history, science, and the classics while boarding with Maury's family. Jefferson came to know various Native Americans including Cherokee chief Ostenaco, who often stopped at Shadwell to visit on their way to Williamsburg to trade.

The legacy of Thomas Jefferson outlived the circumstances that produced it. In Williamsburg, the young Jefferson met and came to admire Patrick Henry. Thomas's father died in 1757, and his estate was divided between his sons, Thomas and Randolph.

Few lives travel as far as that of Thomas Jefferson, and the distance is the point. Thomas inherited approximately 5,000 acres (7.8 sq mi; 20.2 km2), which included the land on which he later built Monticello in 1772. In 1761, at the age of seventeen, Jefferson entered the College of William & Mary in Williamsburg, where he studied mathematics and philosophy with William Small.

The childhood of Thomas Jefferson contains the adult in small print. Under Small's tutelage, Jefferson encountered the ideas of British empiricists, including John Locke, Francis Bacon, and Isaac Newton. Small, Wythe, and Fauquier recognized Jefferson as a man of exceptional ability and included him in their inner circle, where he became a regular member of their Friday dinner parties.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Thomas Jefferson — in that order. Jefferson later wrote that, while there, he "heard more common good sense, more rational & philosophical conversations than in all the rest of my life". The turning point in the life of Thomas Jefferson looked like a failure at the time. He read the law under Wythe's tutelage while working as a law clerk in his office. Jefferson was well-read in a broad variety of subjects, including law, philosophy, history, natural law, natural religion, ethics, and several areas of science, including astronomy and agriculture.

Every biography of Thomas Jefferson has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Jefferson kept two commonplace books: from about age 15 to 30, he compiled a book of sayings and quotations, published in the 20th century as Jefferson's Literary Commonplace Book. During his years of legal study under Wythe, Jefferson began recording his notes on law, history, and philosophy, and continued to do so until the end of his life; his Legal Commonplace Book was also published in the 20th century.

The education of Thomas Jefferson happened mostly outside any school. On July 20, 1765, Jefferson's sister Martha married his close friend and college companion Dabney Carr, which greatly pleased Jefferson. In October of that year, however, Jefferson's sister Jane unexpectedly died at age 25.

What Thomas Jefferson wanted at the start and what Thomas Jefferson got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Her death plunged Jefferson into a months-long period of mourning that was spoken of amongst the family. Jefferson treasured his books and amassed three sizable libraries in his lifetime.

The defining trait of Thomas Jefferson was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Wythe was so impressed with Jefferson that he later bequeathed his entire library to him. In 1770, however, Jefferson's first library was destroyed in a fire at his Shadwell home.

Those who met Thomas Jefferson at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. After British forces set the Library of Congress on fire in the burning of Washington in 1814, Jefferson sold his second library to the U.S. government for $23,950, hoping to help jumpstart the Library of Congress's rebuilding. Jefferson used a portion of the proceeds to pay off some of his large debt.

The private years of Thomas Jefferson explain the public decades better than any speech. In a letter to John Adams, Jefferson wrote, "I cannot live without books." By the time of Jefferson's death a decade later, his third and final library had grown to nearly 2,000 volumes. In 1767, Jefferson was granted admission to the Virginia bar, and lived with his mother at Shadwell.

The family Thomas Jefferson came from matters more than the legends admit. Between 1769 and 1775, he represented Albemarle County in Virginia's House of Burgesses. While serving in the House of Burgesses, Jefferson pursued reforms to slavery, including writing and sponsoring legislation in 1769 to strip power from the royal governor and courts, instead providing masters of slaves with the discretion to emancipate them.

The first real success of Thomas Jefferson arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Jefferson persuaded his cousin Richard Bland to spearhead the legislation's passage, but it faced strong opposition in a state whose economy was largely agrarian. As a lawyer, Jefferson took on seven freedom-seeking enslaved people as clients and waived his fee for one he claimed should be freed before the minimum statutory age for emancipation.

The last chapter of Thomas Jefferson was written long after the fame. As a consolation, Jefferson gave his client some money, which was conceivably used to aid his escape shortly thereafter. Jefferson's underlying intellectual argument that all people were entitled by their creator to what he labeled a "natural right" to liberty is a theme that he later prominently incorporated into the Declaration of Independence.

The whole life of Thomas Jefferson reads like a single decision repeated. In 1767, Jefferson took on 68 cases for the General Court of Virginia and was counsel in three notable cases of that era, Howell v. In 1774, Jefferson authored a resolution calling for a boycott of all British goods in protest of the British Parliament's passing of the Intolerable Acts.

Between the birth and the legend of Thomas Jefferson lie the years that actually decide it. Jefferson's resolution was later expanded into A Summary View of the Rights of British America, published that year in which he argued that people have the right to govern themselves. In 1768, Jefferson began constructing his primary residence, Monticello, on a hilltop overlooking his 5,000-acre (20 km2; 7.8 mi2) plantation.

The reputation of Thomas Jefferson was built in the middle, not at the edges. He spent most of his adult life designing Monticello and was quoted as saying, "Architecture is my delight, and putting up, and pulling down, one of my favorite amusements." Construction was done mostly by local masons and carpenters, assisted by Jefferson's slaves. Turning Monticello into a neoclassical masterpiece in the Palladian style became Jefferson's lifelong project.

Somebody like Thomas Jefferson should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. On January 1, 1772, Jefferson married his third cousin, Martha Wayles Skelton, a 23-year-old widow of Bathurst Skelton. Historian Dumas Malone described the marriage as the happiest period of Jefferson's life.

The life of Thomas Jefferson begins far from where the story usually starts. Martha was a skilled pianist; Jefferson often accompanied her on the violin or cello. During their ten-year marriage, Martha bore six children: Martha "Patsy" (1772–1836); Jane Randolph (1774–1775); an unnamed son who lived for only a few weeks in 1777; Mary "Polly" (1778–1804); Lucy Elizabeth (1780–1781); and another Lucy Elizabeth (1782–1784).

Thomas Jefferson was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Martha's father, John Wayles, died in 1773, and the couple inherited 135 enslaved people, 11,000 acres (45 km2; 17 mi2), and the estate's debts. The debts took Jefferson years to satisfy, contributing to his financial problems.

To understand where Thomas Jefferson ended up, start with where Thomas Jefferson began. Martha later suffered from ill health, including diabetes, and frequent childbirth weakened her. A few months after the birth of her last child, she died on September 6, 1782, with Jefferson at her bedside.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Thomas Jefferson ran through years nobody filmed. Shortly before her death, Martha made Jefferson promise never to marry again, telling him that she could not bear to have another mother raise her children. Jefferson was grief-stricken by her death, relentlessly pacing back and forth for roughly three weeks, and finally emerging to take long rambling rides on secluded roads with his daughter, Martha, who said she was "a solitary witness to many a violent burst of grief".
